topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European public health context; competency frameworks may have limited direct application to Australian organisational settings or non-health sectors, though foundational AI literacy principles may transfer.
takeaways: Competency frameworks for digital/AI literacy in regulated sectors (like health) identify specific technical, ethical, and governance skills beyond basic tool use — consider mapping which of these transferable competencies are most relevant for your employee population.

European public health frameworks emphasise compliance and risk management alongside capability-building; ensure your AI literacy program addresses both technical skills and organisational governance requirements specific to your industry.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Likely limited to public health education contexts; unclear whether findings generalise to other sectors or disciplines without additional detail on study scope and methodology.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption in public health education can be transformed through structured development programmes — design training that moves staff from defensive positions to practical capability-building rather than attempting immediate integration.

Position faculty development as the foundational lever for institutional AI literacy rather than focusing solely on student learning — this addresses the gatekeeper role educators play in shaping organisational readiness.

articles.title: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies - Sage Journals
articles.snippet: Bridging the AI skills gap: Preparing generation Z for the evolving job market landscape through innovative educational strategies  Sage Journals
articles.generalisability: Moderate — addresses Gen Z and educational strategies broadly, but geographic scope and specific educational systems examined are unclear from the title and snippet alone. Applicability may vary by country's education policy and labour market structures.
takeaways: Identify which AI literacy components are most critical for Gen Z entering your organisation's pipeline, then work with L&D to embed these into early-career onboarding or graduate programs.

Innovative educational strategies for AI skills (e.g. project-based learning, cross-disciplinary modules, real-world problem-solving) can be adapted for internal upskilling programs targeting younger cohorts in your workforce.

Assess your organisation's current AI skills teaching approach — many educational gaps identified for Gen Z also apply to existing employees, creating opportunities for unified capability-building initiatives.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development unclear without access to full article methodology and geographic scope.
takeaways: A holistic digital literacy framework that embeds AI competencies (rather than teaching AI in isolation) may improve foundational understanding — consider how your organisation integrates AI skills into existing digital literacy programs rather than siloing them.

Middle school curricula insights on scaffolding AI concepts could inform how you sequence AI learning for employees with varying technical backgrounds — starting with digital literacy foundations before advanced AI applications.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector which may not directly transfer to corporate employee development contexts, though pedagogical principles have broader application.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your workforce (technical, literacy, or domain-specific) before designing training — higher ed strategies distinguish between these levels and tailor accordingly.

Blend theoretical AI knowledge with hands-on, project-based learning rather than relying on lectures alone — this mirrors effective pedagogical approaches that can be adapted to workplace upskilling programs.
Consider scaffolding AI literacy development across multiple touchpoints (not a one-off workshop) to build sustainable capability, drawing on educational frameworks for progressive skill building.

articles.title: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and validation of a competency-based ladder pathway for AI literacy enhancement among higher vocational students | Scientific Reports  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to higher vocational education context. Findings specific to vocational student populations may not generalise to corporate employee AI development programs, though the competency ladder framework could be adapted.
takeaways: Consider developing a tiered, competency-based progression pathway for your AI capability program rather than one-size-fits-all training — this approach allows employees at different skill levels to advance sequentially.

Validate your AI literacy framework against actual performance outcomes to ensure the competency levels you've defined genuinely distinguish capability — don't assume self-reported understanding matches demonstrated competence.
Use the ladder structure to create transparent career pathways that show employees how AI skills build on one another, which may increase engagement and completion rates in upskilling programs.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability is unclear from the snippet alone — depends on sample size, sector coverage, and geographic scope, which are not detailed in the provided information.
takeaways: Generative AI can create a paradox: while it automates routine knowledge tasks, it may simultaneously reduce employees' motivation to build deeper expertise if they over-rely on AI outputs rather than engaging in active learning.

Organisations should structure AI adoption to preserve 'knowledge friction' — ensuring employees still engage cognitively with problems rather than passively accepting AI-generated answers — to maintain long-term capability development.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings may be context-dependent; paternalistic leadership is more prevalent in certain cultural contexts (e.g. East Asian organisations), so generalisability to Western, more egalitarian organisational structures may be limited. Sample characteristics and geographic scope unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership among employees by involving them in decisions about how AI tools are implemented and adapted to their roles—this sense of ownership can increase their willingness to collaborate effectively with AI systems.

In hierarchical or paternalistic leadership contexts, frame AI adoption as a leader-guided initiative that respects employee expertise; allow employees to 'craft' or customise how they work with AI rather than imposing rigid processes from above.

Create structured opportunities for employees to personalise their AI workflows and contribute ideas for improvement—this autonomy within a supportive leadership framework appears to drive both acceptance and productive human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The impact of artificial intelligence application on employees' job insecurity: the moderating roles of self-efficacy and transformational leadership  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The moderating effects of self-efficacy and transformational leadership likely apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear.
takeaways: Leaders can mitigate AI-driven job insecurity by demonstrating transformational leadership — focusing on vision, individualised support, and intellectual stimulation may help employees feel more secure during AI implementation.
Invest in building employee self-efficacy around AI tools and capabilities; research suggests this buffers against job insecurity concerns when AI is introduced.
When rolling out AI applications, combine leadership development with targeted capability-building to address both psychological and practical dimensions of employee anxiety.

articles.title: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: “Under the Shadow of Uncertainty”: the mediating role of job stress and the AI self-efficacy as a shield in cybersecurity behavior | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — without access to the full article, the geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be confirmed. Results may be specific to the surveyed cybersecurity workforce and may not generalise across sectors or geographic regions.
takeaways: AI self-efficacy acts as a protective factor against the negative effects of job stress on cybersecurity behaviour — building employees' confidence in using AI tools may help maintain secure practices even under high-pressure conditions.

Job stress appears to be a significant mediator in the relationship between uncertainty and cybersecurity behaviour — organisations should assess and mitigate stress levels as part of their security culture strategy, not just technical training.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity on scope — title suggests theoretical or empirical work on psychological capital and AI in workplaces, but geographic and sample details are not evident from the snippet provided. Generalisability depends on study design and participant characteristics not disclosed here.
takeaways: Build psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) in teams using AI tools — these psychological resources can buffer against automation anxiety and unlock innovation potential in algorithm-driven roles.
Frame AI as a job resource rather than a threat; employees with higher psychological capital are better positioned to leverage AI tools creatively and adapt to algorithmic workflows.
Assess and develop psychological capital in your workforce before or during AI implementation — this may be a more effective lever for driving adoption and innovation than technical training alone.

articles.title: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic anxiety: AI, work, and the evolving psychological contract in digital discourse  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on discourse analysis of digital commentary rather than primary empirical research; findings reflect public perception and expressed anxieties rather than validated psychological outcomes, limiting generalisability to actual workplace experience.
takeaways: Employee anxiety about AI adoption often stems from perceived threats to the psychological contract (implicit expectations about job security, autonomy, and fairness); proactively communicate how AI will augment rather than replace roles to reset these expectations.

Digital discourse and social media amplify algorithmic anxiety disproportionately; organisations should monitor and address misconceptions early through transparent, two-way dialogue rather than letting anxiety narratives dominate online conversation.

The psychological contract is shifting as AI integration accelerates; HR and leadership must explicitly revisit and renegotiate expectations around skill development, role boundaries, and job security to maintain employee trust and engagement.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without detailed methodology or empirical grounding. Findings and recommendations may reflect US business school assumptions and may not generalise to Australian workplace contexts or non-elite organisational settings.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption could create skill gaps, then design targeted upskilling interventions before implementation rather than retrofitting after disruption.

Engage employees early in AI change initiatives by framing the technology as a tool that augments rather than replaces their roles — this reduces resistance and helps people adapt their work identities more smoothly.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample characteristics not detailed in the snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance perspective) is likely applicable across contexts, but geographic scope, sector representation, and sample size cannot be assessed from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Organizations implementing AI should anticipate that employees will engage in job crafting as a psychological response — understanding whether adoption triggers approach (seeking new opportunities) or avoidance (withdrawing from tasks) behaviours can help design change management strategies that channel energy productively.

Managers can use the approach-avoidance lens to diagnose why employees craft their roles during AI adoption: those showing avoidance patterns may need reassurance about job security and upskilling support, while approach-oriented employees may be ready to take on higher-value work AI enables.

articles.title: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework - Nature
articles.snippet: Advancing applied behavioral science: the GAP framework  Nature
articles.generalisability: Framework-level generalisability depends on empirical validation; the GAP framework itself is presented as a conceptual model applicable across domains, but the snippet provides insufficient detail to assess evidence base or sector limitations.
takeaways: The GAP framework (likely Goals, Antecedents, Processes) offers a structured approach to designing behaviour change interventions — use it to map the specific goal, identify what precedes the target behaviour, and clarify the mechanism of change before implementation.

Applied behavioural science frameworks work best when they bridge theory and practice; ensure any behaviour change initiative you design specifies measurable outcomes and identifies the actual barriers people face, not just assumed ones.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodological details are not evident from the title and snippet alone. Findings may reflect consulting client base rather than broader workforce populations.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as fundamentally a workforce transformation challenge, not just a technology implementation — this reorientation helps leaders prioritize change management and capability-building alongside technical deployment.

Identify and address workforce readiness gaps early: map current skill levels, reskilling needs, and role evolution required before rolling out AI tools, rather than deploying technology and managing disruption reactively.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey report likely draws on global client work, but specific case examples and organisational contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Frame AI capability development as a business change initiative requiring leadership commitment and structural support, rather than a standalone training programme.
Use change management principles (stakeholder engagement, clear communication of 'why', reinforcement mechanisms) to embed AI upskilling into organisational workflows and culture.
Identify and address resistance to AI adoption by mapping employee concerns and designing targeted interventions that connect AI learning to individual roles and career progression.

articles.title: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Inclusive algorithmic work design: the moderating role of DEI interventions and diversity-supportive culture in AI-driven workplace transformation  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not fully evident from title and snippet. Likely limited by sector focus and geographic scope; DEI intervention effectiveness varies significantly across cultural and organisational contexts.
takeaways: Design AI systems with explicit diversity and inclusion principles embedded from the start — algorithmic fairness alone is insufficient without supportive organisational culture to drive adoption and behaviour change.

Before rolling out AI tools, assess your organisation's existing DEI maturity and culture; interventions are most effective when combined with genuine commitment to diversity-supportive practices, not as standalone compliance measures.

Use DEI initiatives as active moderators of AI implementation — they can reduce resistance to algorithmic decision-making and help employees see AI as a tool that supports rather than undermines inclusive work practices.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When personality meets surprise: individual differences in memory for unexpected events  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — generalisability depends on sample size, recruitment method, and whether findings replicate across cultures and age groups.
takeaways: Some personality types are naturally better at remembering things that catch them off guard — suggesting that how we're wired affects what sticks in our minds, not just what we consciously pay attention to.
The finding is counterintuitive: you might expect everyone to remember surprising moments equally well, but personality shapes memory formation in unexpected ways.
This hints at why eyewitness accounts vary so much — personality differences mean two people witnessing the same shocking event may encode and recall it quite differently.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail about sample size, geographic scope, or methodology to assess generalisability.
takeaways: Wine review language patterns can reveal personality traits — what you write about wine apparently says something about who you are.
AI can uncover hidden personality signals in everyday consumer behaviour like food and beverage preferences, suggesting our tastes are more psychologically revealing than we might assume.

This finding shows how machine learning applied to seemingly trivial writing (reviews) can extract psychological insights, making it a fun example of AI finding meaning in places we don't usually look.

articles.title: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people - ScienceDaily
articles.snippet: Brain scans reveal a shocking difference between psychopaths and other people  ScienceDaily
articles.generalisability: Limited — headline claims of 'shocking differences' based on brain imaging require verification of original research methodology, sample size, and whether findings are replicable across populations.
takeaways: Brain imaging studies on psychopathy often rely on small, incarcerated samples that may not represent the broader population of people with psychopathic traits.
The popular framing of 'shocking brain differences' between groups tends to oversimplify complex neuroscience — structural or functional variations don't neatly predict behaviour or moral capacity.

Psychopathy exists on a spectrum and shows up differently across contexts; sensational headlines about 'shocking differences' often obscure the messy reality of how brains and personalities actually work.

articles.title: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs - PsyPost
articles.snippet: How a twin study untangled the surprising roots of authoritarian political beliefs  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on twin sample composition and country of origin, which are not detailed in the snippet. Twin studies typically assume equal environments for monozygotic and dizygotic twins, which may not always hold.
takeaways: Authoritarian political beliefs have a heritable component — genetics appear to influence susceptibility to authoritarian worldviews, not just environment or ideology.
The 'surprising' angle likely challenges the assumption that political authoritarianism is purely learned or chosen, suggesting personality and temperament play an underestimated role.
This reveals why political persuasion often fails: people may have innate predispositions toward authority-seeking or conformity that shape which ideas resonate with them.

articles.title: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Surprising link found between hyperthyroidism and dark personality traits  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — appears to report on a finding but lacks detail on study scope, sample size, or geographic location. Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to the underlying research.
takeaways: A physiological condition (hyperthyroidism) has been linked to personality traits typically associated with narcissism and psychopathy — a surprising connection between endocrinology and psychology.
This finding is counterintuitive because it suggests personality expression may have a metabolic or hormonal foundation, not just psychological or environmental roots.
The link raises an intriguing question: do thyroid imbalances shape behaviour, or do certain personality types have different thyroid profiles? The causal direction remains an open puzzle.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — appears to be a cross-cultural study examining universal patterns in music preference and personality, though specific sample size and demographic details are not evident from the snippet.
takeaways: Personality traits predict music taste in surprisingly consistent ways across different cultures — suggesting some musical preferences may be a universal human feature rather than purely cultural.
Your playlist might be a more honest personality profile than you think: the study hints that what we listen to reveals stable patterns about who we are, regardless of where we're from.
This finding challenges the assumption that musical taste is entirely learned and shaped by local culture — there appear to be underlying personality-driven patterns that transcend geography.

topics.label: Psychological Safety
topics.description: Research on psychological safety and its role in team learning, AI experimentation, and innovation.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to academic settings and multicultural team contexts; generalisability to corporate or other organisational sectors unclear from snippet provided.
takeaways: AI tools can be designed to prompt or support inclusive leadership behaviours; explore how algorithmic nudges or decision-support systems might help leaders recognise and address gender dynamics in your own diverse teams.

Gendered outcomes in multicultural teams may be influenced by how leadership practices are structured or assisted; audit current team processes to identify where AI-assisted practices could surface hidden biases in hiring, task allocation, or recognition.

Psychological safety in diverse teams depends partly on whether inclusive leadership is consistently enacted; consider whether AI-assisted tools could help standardise inclusive practices across multiple team leaders or locations.

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate — PwC surveys typically cover multiple countries and sectors, but sample composition, response rates, and whether results are weighted are not evident from the snippet. Findings may skew toward larger organisations and developed economies where PwC operates.
takeaways: Use workforce survey data to identify where psychological safety gaps exist in your organisation — compare your team's confidence in speaking up, reporting concerns, and taking interpersonal risks against PwC's global benchmarks to pinpoint priorities.

When communicating organisational change or AI adoption, address both hopes and fears explicitly; acknowledge worker anxieties (job security, skill relevance) alongside opportunities to build trust and reduce defensive silence.
Monitor shifts in employee sentiment year-on-year using similar questions to track whether psychological safety improvements are taking hold — one-off surveys miss momentum.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability limited by lack of geographic or sectoral detail in snippet; appears to be a single empirical study rather than meta-analysis. Findings on psychological safety and ethical leadership during AI adoption are relevant across contexts, but sample characteristics and size unknown.
takeaways: AI adoption can harm employee mental health if it erodes psychological safety — prioritise creating explicit psychological safety interventions (e.g., safe-to-speak-up norms, non-punitive feedback channels) when rolling out AI tools.

Ethical leadership is protective: leaders who model transparency about AI limitations, acknowledge employee concerns, and involve staff in AI implementation decisions can buffer against depression and disengagement during technological change.

Monitor employee wellbeing during AI transitions using validated mental health measures and psychological safety surveys, and adjust implementation pace or support if depression or withdrawal increases.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG insights are typically based on consulting experience across global clients, but specific sample details, methodology, and geographic scope are not evident from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce disparities in voice and participation across employee groups; assess whether quieter team members (e.g. junior staff, underrepresented groups) feel equally safe speaking up in your workplace.

Use psychological safety as an equity lever: create explicit norms and leader behaviours that signal it's safe to contribute regardless of status or background, then measure changes in contribution patterns over time.

articles.title: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams - SHRM
articles.snippet: 4 Ways Leaders Can Build 'Psychological Safety' in Their Work Teams  SHRM
articles.generalisability: Moderate — SHRM is US-focused; advice on psychological safety principles is generally applicable across contexts, but specific organisational examples or regulatory references may be US-specific.
takeaways: Identify the four concrete leadership behaviours SHRM recommends and assess which are weakest in your current team interactions — use this as a starting point for targeted leadership development.

Psychological safety is built through consistent modelling of vulnerability and non-punitive responses to failure; pick one behaviour to practise deliberately over the next month and measure team response through informal check-ins.
Document how you currently respond when team members raise concerns or admit mistakes — this baseline will help you track progress in shifting toward psychologically safer interactions.

articles.title: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces - Frontiers
articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — article title and snippet do not provide sufficient methodological detail to assess sample size, geographic scope, or sector representation. Full article review needed to determine generalisability.
takeaways: Psychological capital (hope, efficacy, resilience, optimism) may be a lever for fostering innovation and engagement when AI is introduced as a workplace tool — consider assessing and developing these capacities during AI adoption.

Frame AI systems as job resources rather than threats to activate positive psychological states; this framing may reduce defensive reactions and encourage employees to experiment with new capabilities.
Invest in building psychological capital alongside technical AI training — resilience and confidence in one's ability to learn may matter as much as digital skills for successful AI integration.
